newsitem.title: FRANCE: Renault plunges into the red.
newsitem.headline: Renault plunges into the red.

text.p: French carmaker Renault reported a 5.25 billion franc ($923.3 million) loss for 1996 on Thursday, its first shortfall in 10 years, after taking a 3.91 billion franc charge to close down a Belgian plant and cut nearly 2,800 jobs in France.

Belgian workers protesting the closure clashed with French police outside a car depot in the northern French town of Wavrin. Workers also staged demonstrations at an engine plant and outside Renault's Paris headquarters during a board meeting.
Chairman Louis Schweitzer said the board approved the plant shutdown and job cutbacks. The French government is the largest shareholder with a 46 percent stake.

"Stopping a company like Renault from closing a plant that doesn't correspond to the current state of competition would put the whole company at risk and tens of thousands of jobs," Prime Minister Alain Juppe said on TFI television. He said he was glad Renault had begun talks with unions on easing the blow.
Renault increased the provision set aside for the closure by 400 million francs to 2.8 billion to help the plant's 3,100 workers through layoff or retraining benefits.
Schweitzer also said the closure would take place during 1997, signalling some flexibility to union demands to keep the assembly plant open beyond the original end-July deadline.

Even excluding the restructuring charges, Renault had an operating loss of 1.77 billion francs, compared with a year-earlier operating profit of 1.20 billion francs, as both its car and truck operations lost money.
"The car division was especially hurt by a price war that spread in France during a year of major model renewal," the company said in its earnings statement.

The car branch's operating loss, including restructuring charges, ballooned to 6.55 billion francs last year from a restated loss of 991 million in 1995 despite the huge success of the new Megane Scenic, a hybrid between a car and minivan.

The industrial vehicles division, which had earned 978 million francs in 1995, swung to a 705 million franc deficit last year because U.S. and European truck sales fell. The division owns Mack Trucks of the United States.
"In the United States, that (downturn) was expected, but in Europe it was not," Schweitzer told reporters. "We were expecting a recovery but it stalled."
The company's financial services division contributed an operating profit of 1.26 billion francs last year, slightly under its 1995 profit of 1.27 billion.
Schweitzer said the group was aiming for breakeven at the car division in 1997 unless the French car market fell more than the roughly 10 percent drop forecast by industry experts.
The truck business is expected to keep losing money and will be the focus of more cost-cutting measures, he said. The financial services branch should turn in about the same performance as last year.
"This would bring the group...to operating profit" for 1997, he said. "The net depends on exceptionals."
Renault's 1996 charges include 2.8 billion francs for the Vilvoorde plant closure announced on February 27 and 940 million for 2,764 job cuts planned in France this year.

In Paris, about 100 Renault workers demonstrated outside the company's headquarters. Police also turned away a group of workers who tried to enter the company's prestige showroom on the Champs-Elysees avenue.
But workers have so far shown lukewarm response to union calls for labour action despite a reputation for militancy.
Renault, the smallest of the six companies producing a full range of cars in Europe, has cut its workforce by around 40,000 in the past 10 years to just under 141,000 at the end of 1996.

Schweitzer has said the shutdown is essential to streamline Renault's car assembly operations in Europe. He said they were too dispersed among plants that are much smaller and costlier to run than those of its rivals.
The car division began losing money in the second half of 1995, although Renault reported a full-year profit of 2.14 billion francs, underpinned by its truck and financial services businesses.

Renault's last annual loss was for 1986, when it reported a loss of 5.85 billion francs. In the two preceding years, it lost 23.5 billion francs in the company's worst postwar crisis. ($= 5.686 French Francs)
